India climbed from the bottom half of th.takeaway: In 2015, at 81st of 141, India ranked ahead of 43 per cent of the other economies. In 2026, at 38th of 139, it ranks ahead of 73 per cent.
India climbed from the bottom half of th.detail: The Global Innovation Index has covered between 125 and 143 economies, so a rank alone is hard to compare across years. This line shows India's position as the share of the other ranked economies it sits ahead of. India slid from 62nd in 2011 to 81st in 2015, then climbed every year to 38th in 2025 and 2026. The shaded band is the range of ranks the European Commission's auditors find when they vary the index's choices, converted to the same scale.
India climbed from the bottom half of th.whyShowThis: It is the rank everyone quotes, drawn so that years with different numbers of economies sit fairly on one line, with its uncertainty showing.
India climbed from the bottom half of th.howToRead: Higher is better. A point at 73 means India ranks ahead of 73 per cent of the other economies that year. The marked years are editions where the number of economies changed sharply.
India climbed from the bottom half of th.mistakeToAvoid: WIPO says scores and ranks are not directly comparable between editions, because the indicators, the data and the list of economies change. Read the long climb, not the step between any two years.
India climbed from the bottom half of th.mobileNote: Read the line's level at the start and the end; the band shows how uncertain each year's position is.

India's outputs have outranked its input.takeaway: India has always ranked better on what comes out of its economy than on what goes in: 44th on outputs and 87th on inputs in 2011, 25th and 49th in 2026.
India's outputs have outranked its input.detail: The index is two halves averaged together. Inputs cover institutions, education and research, infrastructure, credit and markets, and business sophistication. Outputs cover knowledge and technology, such as patents, papers and high-tech exports, and creative work, such as trademarks, designs and cultural exports. Both lines have risen and the gap between them has narrowed, but outputs have stayed ahead in all sixteen editions.
India's outputs have outranked its input.whyShowThis: The gap explains why India ranks better overall than its research base alone would suggest.
India's outputs have outranked its input.howToRead: Each line is India's position on one half of the index, as the share of other economies it ranks ahead of. Higher is better.
India's outputs have outranked its input.mistakeToAvoid: Strong outputs on weaker inputs can mean efficiency, or it can mean a few large strengths, IT services above all, carrying the average. The chart alone cannot tell them apart.
India's outputs have outranked its input.mobileNote: The upper line is outputs, the lower inputs; watch the space between them.

India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.takeaway: When the index's choices are varied, India's 2026 rank ranges from 34th to 39th, overlapping Malaysia, Slovenia, Hungary, Bulgaria and Poland.
India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.detail: The European Commission's Joint Research Centre audits the index each year. It reruns the calculation thousands of times with different weights and different ways of filling missing data, and records the range covering 90 per cent of the results. India's range is six places wide. For 86 of the 139 economies the range is 10 places or fewer.
India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.whyShowThis: A rank looks exact. This shows how much of it is fixed by the data and how much by the method.
India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.howToRead: Each bar is an economy's range of possible ranks; the dot is its published rank. Bars that overlap are hard to tell apart.
India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read a move of one or two places as news. India at 36th or 39th next year would be within this year's range.
India's 38th could be anywhere from 34th.mobileNote: India is the row in black; compare its bar with the rows just above and below.

India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.takeaway: India's 38th averages ranks as high as 1st, for ICT services exports, and as low as 115th, for foreign students in its universities.
India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.detail: Each dot is one of the 77 indicators where India has a value in 2026. India is in the top 10 on five of them and the top 20 on fifteen, and in the bottom half on 25. Its median rank is 48th. The best ranks are about size and markets: ICT services exports, domestic market size, late-stage venture capital deals, unicorn valuations. The worst are about people per head: researchers, knowledge-intensive jobs, women with advanced degrees, foreign students.
India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.whyShowThis: It shows what the single number is made of, and that India's profile is lopsided rather than middling.
India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.howToRead: Further right is a better rank. Blue dots are input indicators, green dots output indicators.
India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.mistakeToAvoid: The indicators are not equally weighted in the final score, and two of India's best eleven ranks come from expert-opinion surveys rather than counted data.
India is in the world's top 20 on 15 mea.mobileNote: Dots on the right are India's world-class measures; dots on the left are its weakest.

Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.takeaway: India scores about 10 points above a typical economy. The two output pillars supply about 7.5 of those points, and knowledge and technology outputs alone about 5.
Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.detail: A typical economy here is built from the median score on each pillar across all 139 economies: 30.3 points once weighted. India scores 40.1. Each bar is the gap on one pillar, multiplied by the weight the index gives it: a tenth for each input pillar and a quarter for each output pillar. India is above the median on all seven, but only narrowly on institutions, infrastructure and business sophistication.
Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.whyShowThis: It answers where the 38th comes from, in the index's own arithmetic.
Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.howToRead: Bars add up from left to right to the total at the end. Longer bars contribute more of India's lead.
Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.mistakeToAvoid: No real country has the typical economy's profile; it is a reference point. And output pillars weigh more because there are only two of them, so a strength there counts more.
Three-quarters of India's lead over a ty.mobileNote: The two long bars near the end are the output pillars.

Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.takeaway: On knowledge and technology outputs India went from 34th to 15th between 2022 and 2026. On human capital and research it went from 43rd to 54th.
Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.detail: The 2022 to 2026 databases share a format, so the pillars can be lined up. Most of India's rise on knowledge and technology outputs came in 2023, when WIPO replaced new businesses per person (India 114th) with unicorn valuation (India 9th). India also improved on creative outputs and on infrastructure, from 78th to 62nd. It slipped on institutions, human capital and research, market sophistication and business sophistication; most of the market sophistication fall came in 2025, when WIPO replaced its venture capital measures.
Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.whyShowThis: It shows which parts of the index are driving the recent climb, and which are not.
Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.howToRead: Each row is a pillar. The open end is 2022 and the dot is 2026, both as the share of other economies India ranks ahead of. A red dot means India's standing fell.
Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.mistakeToAvoid: Indicators change between editions even within a pillar, and the table grew from 132 to 139 economies. The biggest moves on this chart, up and down, are partly changes of indicator.
Since 2022, India has risen on both outp.mobileNote: Green and blue dots mark rises; red dots mark falls.

In the world's top ten by total, far low.takeaway: India is 3rd in the world for scientific articles and 89th per person; 5th for resident patent filings and 38th per person; 8th for researchers and 83rd per person.
In the world's top ten by total, far low.detail: Each measure is ranked twice among the economies with data: by the national total and per person. India is in the top ten by total on all five: patent filings (2024), scientific and technical articles (2023), researchers (2020), R&D spending at purchasing power (2020) and ICT services exports (2025, second to Ireland). Per person it falls to between 38th and 89th.
In the world's top ten by total, far low.whyShowThis: A country of 1.46 billion people looks large on any total. Per person is the other half of the picture, and the index itself mostly divides by GDP, not by people.
In the world's top ten by total, far low.howToRead: Each row is a measure. The open end is India's standing by total, the dot per person, both as the share of economies with data that India ranks ahead of.
In the world's top ten by total, far low.mistakeToAvoid: Per person is not automatically the right measure: a large total can support things a small one cannot, such as specialised labs or a deep startup market. The point is that both are true at once.
In the world's top ten by total, far low.mobileNote: The gap in each row is the difference between India's size and its depth.

For its income, India scores well above.takeaway: India's GII score is about 13.5 points above what its income per person would predict, the eighth-largest margin of the 139 economies.
For its income, India scores well above.detail: Richer countries score higher; across all 139 economies the correlation between the score and income per person (on a log scale) is 0.81. India, with GDP per person of about $12,100 at purchasing power, scores 40.1. The seven economies further above the line are China, Switzerland, Sweden, South Korea, the United Kingdom, the United States and Finland. WIPO has called India an innovation overperformer in every edition since 2011, a record it shares only with Viet Nam.
For its income, India scores well above.whyShowThis: It is the strongest case for India's 38th: it is very good for a lower-middle-income country.
For its income, India scores well above.howToRead: Each dot is an economy. Left to right is income per person, each step multiplying it; up is a higher score. The line is the average relation.
For its income, India scores well above.mistakeToAvoid: Above the line does not mean above the rich world. India's score is still below every economy ranked in the top 37, though it beats 33 of the 35 upper-middle-income economies.
For its income, India scores well above.mobileNote: Find India's labelled dot and compare its height with the line beneath it.

Five of India's research figures in the.takeaway: Of India's 77 values in the 2026 index, five describe 2020, and all five are about research spending and researchers.
Five of India's research figures in the.detail: The index draws on the latest data each source has. For India, 30 values describe 2024, 29 describe 2025 and three describe 2026. The five 2020 values are R&D spending as a share of GDP, R&D performed by business, R&D financed by business, researchers per million people and the share of researchers working in business. UNESCO, the source, had nothing newer for India when the edition was compiled.
Five of India's research figures in the.whyShowThis: It shows that the index's verdict on India's research base is six years old.
Five of India's research figures in the.howToRead: Each bar counts India's indicators whose latest value describes that year.
Five of India's research figures in the.mistakeToAvoid: Old data is not necessarily wrong data, and newer Indian figures are not on the same basis. See the next section.
Five of India's research figures in the.mobileNote: The bar at 2020 is the research data; most of the rest is from 2024 and 2025.

Even on its new survey, India spends les.takeaway: India spent 0.65 per cent of GDP on research in 2020 by UNESCO's count, and 0.84 per cent in 2023-24 by its own new survey. The world spends about 2.6 per cent.
Even on its new survey, India spends les.detail: Gross expenditure on R&D covers research done in a country by government, business, universities and non-profits. Among the peers shown, South Korea spends 4.9 per cent, China 2.6, Türkiye 1.4 and Brazil 1.2. Viet Nam, at 0.41 per cent, and Indonesia, the Philippines and Mexico spend less than India. Years differ by country and are printed with each name.
Even on its new survey, India spends les.whyShowThis: Research spending is the input the index cannot see past 2020 for India, checked here against India's own newer figure.
Even on its new survey, India spends les.howToRead: Each bar is one economy's R&D spending as a share of its GDP in its latest year. India appears twice: UNESCO's 2020 figure and DST's 2023-24 figure.
Even on its new survey, India spends les.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the two India bars as growth. DST's new figure comes from a different, wider survey, and the two are not on the same basis.
Even on its new survey, India spends les.mobileNote: India's two bars sit near the middle; the world average is near the top.

India has fewer researchers per person t.takeaway: India had 259 full-time researchers per million people in 2020. China had about 2,100 in 2023 and the world about 1,650.
India has fewer researchers per person t.detail: Researchers are counted as full-time equivalents, so two people each spending half their time on research count as one. India's 2020 count is the lowest among the peers shown, below Indonesia (395), the Philippines (320) and Viet Nam (836). South Korea has about 9,500 per million. DST's new survey counts 354 for India in 2023-24 on a wider basis, which would place it above only the Philippines.
India has fewer researchers per person t.whyShowThis: People are what research money buys, and the per-person count is where India is furthest behind.
India has fewer researchers per person t.howToRead: Each bar is researchers per million people in that economy's latest year, printed with the name.
India has fewer researchers per person t.mistakeToAvoid: Brazil's latest figure is from 2014 and India's from 2020, so this is a comparison of latest available years, not of one year.

India's share of the world's ICT service.takeaway: India sold 12.7 per cent of the world's ICT services exports in 2005, 17.2 per cent in 2012 and 13.9 per cent in 2024.
India's share of the world's ICT service.detail: ICT services cover computer services, telecommunications and related work sold abroad. In dollars India's exports rose from about $23 billion in 2005 to about $200 billion in 2025, second only to Ireland's. But world exports grew almost as fast, so India's share rose until 2012, fell to 12.6 per cent in 2021 and has recovered only partly since.
India's share of the world's ICT service.whyShowThis: This is the indicator on which India ranks first in the world, read over twenty years.
India's share of the world's ICT service.howToRead: One line: India's exports of ICT services divided by the world's, each year.
India's share of the world's ICT service.mistakeToAvoid: A steady share is not stagnation in money terms; the industry grew about ninefold. It means the rest of the world's ICT services grew at a similar pace.
India's share of the world's ICT service.mobileNote: The peak is in 2012; the latest point is lower.

India's four clusters are large, but spr.takeaway: Bengaluru is the world's 25th-largest innovation cluster and 83rd of the 100 by intensity per person. Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai are 96th, 97th and 98th by intensity.
India's four clusters are large, but spr.detail: WIPO finds clusters by mapping where patent inventors, scientific authors and venture capital deals are located, then ranks the top 100 by their share of the world's activity. India has four. Bengaluru (1.8 per cent of world activity), Delhi (1.6), Mumbai (1.1) and Chennai (0.6). Divided by population, each falls near the bottom of the 100, because each covers a very large population, more than 31 million people in WIPO's Delhi cluster.
India's four clusters are large, but spr.whyShowThis: Invention concentrates in cities. This places India's cities against the world's, by size and by density.
India's four clusters are large, but spr.howToRead: Each dot is a cluster. Further right is a larger share of world activity, on a log scale; higher is more activity per person.
India's four clusters are large, but spr.mistakeToAvoid: WIPO's clusters are drawn from where inventors and authors live, not city boundaries, and its method changed in 2023 and 2025. Compare only 2025 and 2026 ranks.
India's four clusters are large, but spr.mobileNote: India's four dots sit to the middle-left and low down.

Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.takeaway: Among eleven middle-income economies, India was fourth by GII score in 2022, behind China, Malaysia and Türkiye, and third in 2026.
Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.detail: In the full table India went from 40th to 38th. Indonesia made the biggest move, from 75th to 55th. Viet Nam climbed from 48th to 43rd and the Philippines from 59th to 52nd. Türkiye fell from 37th to 45th and Mexico from 58th to 65th. China stayed first in the group, at 11th and 10th in the world.
Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.whyShowThis: Economies at a similar stage are a fairer comparison than the top of the table.
Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.howToRead: The left column is the order among these eleven in 2022, the right column in 2026. Lines join each economy's two places; blue lines rose two or more places, red lines fell two or more, and India's is black.
Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.mistakeToAvoid: The order is by score among these eleven only, and the full table grew from 132 to 139 economies over the period.
Among eleven peers, India moved from fou.mobileNote: Follow India's line from left to right.

India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.takeaway: India ranks 15th on knowledge and technology outputs, Viet Nam 35th. Viet Nam ranks 48th on business sophistication, India 63rd.
India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.detail: India and Viet Nam are the two economies WIPO has called innovation overperformers in every edition since 2011. Their profiles differ. India leads on knowledge and technology outputs and on human capital and research. Viet Nam leads on business sophistication, creative outputs and market sophistication, and is first in the world on high-technology exports as a share of trade. China leads both on every pillar, by a wide margin on all but institutions.
India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.whyShowThis: It shows that a strong rank for its income can come from very different economies.
India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.howToRead: Three bars per pillar, for India, Viet Nam and China, each the share of the 139 economies that country ranks ahead of, printed above the bar. Taller is better.
India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.mistakeToAvoid: Pillar ranks average many indicators. A lead on a pillar can rest on one or two of them.
India leads Viet Nam on knowledge output.mobileNote: Compare the first two bars in each group: India and Viet Nam.

Universities now file more than half of.takeaway: Indian applicants filed 68,201 patent applications in 2024-25, five times as many as in 2016-17. Educational institutions filed 37,681 of them, 55 per cent.
Universities now file more than half of.detail: The bands split Indian filings at the Indian Patent Office by type of applicant. Educational institutions appear only from 2021-22, when an 80 per cent fee cut made them a category of their own; before that they filed among companies, labs and other organisations. Taken together, those two groups went from 11,150 applications in 2020-21 to 45,776 in 2024-25. Individuals filed 17,170 in 2024-25 and startups and small firms about 5,300.
Universities now file more than half of.whyShowThis: Patents are the output indicator that has risen fastest for India, and who files them changes what the rise means.
Universities now file more than half of.howToRead: Each band is one type of applicant, stacked; the top edge is all Indian filings that year. Years are financial years, shown by their first calendar year: 2024 is 2024-25.
Universities now file more than half of.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the green band's appearance in 2021 as universities starting to file. The category was new; their earlier filings sit in the blue band. An application is not a granted patent, and the counts say nothing about why any institution files.
Universities now file more than half of.mobileNote: The green band at the top right is universities and colleges.

Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.takeaway: Tamil Nadu filed about 200 patent applications per million people in 2024-25, Punjab 143 and Karnataka 122. Bihar filed about 2.5.
Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.detail: Counts are by the applicant's state, divided by projected population. Tamil Nadu filed 15,440 applications, more than any state, and is home to three of the ten largest academic filers: Saveetha, Sathyabama and VIT. Punjab is home to Lovely Professional University, the largest single filer. Chandigarh, a small union territory, has the highest rate of all, 230 per million. Puducherry is in the data but too small to draw.
Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.whyShowThis: It is the closest thing to a state-level view of invention that official data allows; WIPO's index has no state figures.
Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.howToRead: Darker states file more applications per person. Hover or tap a state for its figure.
Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.mistakeToAvoid: An application is recorded at the applicant's address, so a university or company's filings count in its home state wherever the inventors work. The map measures where applicants are registered, not where inventing happens.
Tamil Nadu files 80 times as many patent.mobileNote: The darkest states are in the south and the north-west.

India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.takeaway: On DST's earlier survey India spent 0.64 per cent of GDP on R&D in 2020-21. On the new survey it spent 0.83 per cent in 2021-22.
India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.detail: From 2021-22 DST's figures come from a National Science and Technology Survey, a census of more than 8,000 institutions, which counts private universities as a separate line and draws on wider company data. Before that, university research for 2018-19 to 2020-21 had been estimated by projecting forward old growth rates. Measured private-sector R&D rose by almost 80 per cent across the break, and 2020-21 was a low base, with central-government R&D down during the pandemic. DST did not recompute the earlier years, so the two lines cannot be joined.
India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.whyShowThis: Some of the rise comes from counting more, and this is the most likely misreading of India's new figures.
India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.howToRead: Two separate lines, one for each survey design. Fiscal years are shown by their first calendar year: 2021 is 2021-22.
India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read the step between the lines as growth alone. DST's projections for 2024-25 and 2025-26 are left out because they are estimates, not survey results.
India's R&D share jumped in 2021-22, the.mobileNote: The gap between the two lines is a change of method.
